Hey! I know it's not terribly original, but I thought a simple discussion would be nice to help this subverse take off a little more! I'm not talking about Pokemon Generation, just region (cities, routes, gyms, caves, etc.). For example, your favorite region might be Hoenn because you love the water, Fortree City, Sootopolis City, and Norman, but you prefer Kanto for the Pokemon, and Unova for the story, etc...
What's your favorite Pokemon region and why?

Personally, my favorite region is Johto.

A big part of it is because of nostalgia for sure. One of my favorite cities is Ecruteak City and Bell Tower (especially in Heart Gold/Soul Silver; the autumn leaves are beautiful). Tohjo Falls, Lake of Rage, Goldenrod City, and Mt. Silver are some other cool locations. The special apricorn balls are really fun/cool too.

Morty is also one of my favorite gym leaders (he's really hot, I mean, has a cool personality and seems to play a big role in Ecruteak City). Finally, the Kansai region of Japan (which Johto is based off of), is one of the most beautiful places. I've been to Kyoto/Osaka twice (I studied abroad in Japan, and since I live in Korea I usually stop by Japan once a year for a few days). I have a lot of great memories there, especially traveling around Arashiyama.

Speaking as a fellow dev who released his app strictly on Lollipop and then decided to go back and rewrite the entire codebase with the support libraries, I would strongly advise you to save yourself the inevitable headaches and to start using the support libraries now while it's still early.

Unlike iOS, 80% of the entire Android user base is still behind on old versions (do not underestimate how slow the trend to upgrade has been and will continue to be). Also, the AppCompat libraries work in a way that if you're using Lollipop, it'll automatically switch to using the native libraries, so there's exactly no difference for Lollipop users. Other devs have also mentioned that Google actually spends more time polishing the support libraries than they do with the latest due to the fact that the support libraries affect the huge majority of Android users. In other words, there's been reported cases of bugs in the latest library, but were first fixed in the support libraries before they were in the latest.

I've read it is an extremely hot gas, ionized or something (what are ions, btw?), but that's hard to understand in a simple manner. We all know many examples of gas, solid and liquid, but plasma...? It loops my mind.
What is PLASMA and is it true that fire is made of it?

Alright, so you already know solid, liquid and gas, but let's review quickly including some building blocks.

  • Particles: proton (positive charge), neutron (neutral charge), and electron (negative charge).

  • Atoms: made up of particles and have neutral charge. For example, a Beryllium (Be) atom has 4 protons (+4), 5 neutrons (±0), and 4 electrons (-4).

  • Ions: An ion is just an electrically charged atom (or group of atoms). So if I have my Beryllium atom with 4 electrons and one is removed, I'm left with a Beryllium atom that has an extra positive charge [+4 (protons) ±0 (neutrons) -3 (electrons) = +1] and a free electron. Since the atom is charged, it's not exactly Beryllium anymore, but a Beryllium ion.

    Ions are denoted by the chemical symbol and a superscript charge. So in this case I would have Be1+ (usually written without the '1' like Be+). If 2 electrons were removed I'd have Be2+. If we go the other way by adding electrons, then the atom becomes negatively charged; with 5 electrons we'd have Be1- (Be-) and with 6 electrons we'd have Be2-. Notice the "other way" is adding electrons, not remove protons - that would make it a different atom altogether.

    As I mentioned, the charge could be over a group of atoms also, so I could have a Carbon atom and a (-1) Nitrogen ion and create CN-, which is also known as Cyanide. There are reasons why some ions exist and why some don't, but that's out of the scope of this discussion.

Thanks for hanging in there... we're almost done!

  • Solid: atoms are tightly bound to one another which gives it a "structure." There's no flow of atoms.

  • Liquid: atoms are attracted to one another, but not enough to provide any structure. They can flow around one another.

  • Gas: atoms are independent of one another and move freely.

Okay really brief pause for a reminder. When something (like water) is going through the states of matter, the difference is the energy (temperature). If you have solid water (ice) and heat it, you get liquid water. Heat it up more and you get gas water (vapor).

  • Plasma: state of matter where the matter is broken into positively charged ions and negatively charged electrons. Basically, you put enough energy into a gas (usually thermally) and it's too much for the atoms/molecules to handle so electrons start flying out of their orbits and you end up with a "hot soup" of ions and electrons.

So I used water as an example before. Turns out, if you add enough energy to water vapor you get water plasma. A few years ago some researchers were able to generate pure H2O plasma for a very short amount of time: PDF Results. Not too long after, researchers discovered a planet that has a water atmosphere where the pressure and heat are so intense at the lower levels that it's water plasma: Source.

There are many more common forms of plasma we experience. A plasma torch is a common tool in workshops and uses a gas (like oxygen) and high voltage to create a small jet of plasma that can cut things very well (I've used one to cut 1/2" stainless steal). Many people have experienced using a Plasma Globe which is a dome filled with a noble gas (usually neon or a mixture) and a high voltage electrode, which creates plasma filaments. Plasma TVs are aptly named because they contain small cells of "electrically charged ionized gases," which is based on what we know is, literally, "plasmas."

I think one thing that confuses people is that we treat plasma like it's exclusive to other things, when really it describes some matter. I can't tell someone to fetch me "liquid" when I want liquid oxygen as I haven't specified which liquid I want. Similarly, I can't request a soda with "solid" at a restaurant without confusing the waiter, when I mean ice (solid water). So in a workshop you might use an oxygen plasma torch, whereas at home you might create neon plasma or xenon plasma by turning on your TV.

Sorry that was kind of long.

tl;dr: plasma is when a gas gets so hot that electrons start flinging about (and any atom/molecule that loses any electrons becomes an ion).

I hope this helped.
